frozen_original.title: USDA/RFK Dietary Guidelines Politicized; NIH Nutrition Research Gutted
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and RFK Jr. announced a 'line-by-line review' of the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee's science report, with Kennedy pledging guidelines as short as four pages — compared to the prior 164-page document — potentially contradicting scientific consensus on saturated fats, seed oils, and red meat. The NIH's lead ultra-processed food researcher resigned in April 2025 after 21 years, citing fear of censorship. The Trump budget proposed cutting NIH nutrition research funding while also eliminating the CDC's National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion ($1.4 billion annual budget). Scientists and CSPI condemned the MAHA Commission's strategy report for including fake citations and pseudoscientific claims, while the administration canceled over $1 billion in local food funding and terminated NIH grants covering nutrition and diet-related disease research.

primary.resolution: The frozen card combines separate March and April events. Two source-supported child drafts are complete. Its other budget, CDC, MAHA citation, local-food funding, and grant claims are separate and not established by the sources accessed; no children are proposed for them.

children.title: USDA and HHS Announce Line-by-Line Review of Dietary Guidelines Report
children.description_short: USDA and HHS announced a line-by-line review of the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee report and set a target to publish final guidelines before the statutory deadline.
children.description_medium: USDA and HHS announced a line-by-line review of the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee’s scientific report on March 11, 2025. The report was advisory, not the final guidelines; officials said they aimed to publish by the statutory deadline. Contemporaneous reporting described the committee’s evidence review and said it made no recommendation on ultra-processed foods.
children.description_long: On March 11, 2025, USDA and HHS announced a line-by-line review of the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee’s scientific report. The committee’s report was an advisory document submitted to the departments; it was not the final federal Dietary Guidelines. USDA and HHS said they aimed to release the 2025–2030 guidelines before the statutory December 31 deadline and described future process improvements on transparency and conflicts of interest. Agri-Pulse reported that the committee spent 22 months reviewing nutrition evidence and that its recommendations included dietary-pattern advice. It also reported that the committee made no recommendation on ultra-processed foods, citing a lack of research. The sourced event is the agencies’ announcement of a review and timetable. The release’s political-science rhetoric does not establish that scientific conclusions were changed for political reasons. This card covers only the review announcement. The frozen parent also mixed in separate budget, CDC, grant, citation, local-food funding, and NIH personnel claims; those are not established by these sources and are not included here.

children.title: NIH Nutrition Researcher Kevin Hall Announces Early Retirement and Alleges Censorship
children.description_short: NIH researcher Kevin Hall announced early retirement and alleged HHS aides censored his work; HHS denied the accusation.
children.description_medium: NIH nutrition researcher Kevin Hall announced an early retirement on April 16, 2025, after 21 years. CBS News reported Hall’s allegations that HHS officials restricted interviews and other research communications. HHS denied censorship and disputed his account. The reports document competing statements, not a finding that officials censored Hall or caused his departure.
children.description_long: On April 16, 2025, NIH nutrition researcher Kevin Hall announced early retirement after 21 years at the agency. CBS News reported that Hall said he was stepping down and accused senior aides to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. of censorship. Hall told CBS that officials blocked a direct interview with a New York Times reporter about his ultra-processed-food research; he also said he was barred from presenting at a conference and faced demanded edits to a manuscript. These are Hall’s reported allegations. HHS denied editing his answers and rejected the censorship charge, saying NIH scientists could discuss research through written responses or other means and that it remained committed to gold-standard research. The Washington Post likewise described Hall’s concerns about political interference at NIH. The available sources establish the retirement announcement and competing accounts, not a factual finding that censorship occurred or that any specific official caused Hall to leave. The dietary-guidelines review is a separate event and is not part of this record.

frozen_original.title: Trump Signs Executive Order Effectively Ending Independent Counsel Statute
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, Trump signed an executive order asserting direct presidential supervisory authority over all Justice Department prosecutions and investigations — including those that had previously been designated as independent special counsel investigations — effectively ending the practical independence of any federal investigation that the President chose to override or terminate. The order claimed the Attorney General and all DOJ prosecutors served at the pleasure of the President and were subject to presidential direction in all matters. Legal scholars noted the order conflicted directly with the independent counsel regulations promulgated under federal law and with the constitutional principle that the executive branch cannot investigate itself. The order was seen as ensuring no independent special counsel could ever again investigate a president or his allies without the president's consent — the lesson Trump drew from his experience with Robert Mueller's investigation.

primary.resolution: The February 18, 2025 order is a real, source-supported action concerning executive supervision and regulatory review. The frozen record’s claim that it ended the independent-counsel statute or abolished special-counsel regulations is removed; the corrected card describes the order’s actual scope.
primary.title: Trump order expands presidential supervision of executive agencies
primary.description_short: Trump order expands presidential supervision of executive agencies
primary.description_medium: On February 18, 2025, the White House published “Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies.” The order states that executive officials are subject to presidential supervision and directs all agencies, including independent agencies, to submit proposed and final significant regulatory actions to OIRA before Federal Register publication. It also makes presidential and Attorney General legal interpretations controlling for executive-branch employees. The text does not establish that an independent-counsel statute was ended.
primary.description_long: On February 18, 2025, the White House published “Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies.” The order states that executive branch officials remain subject to presidential supervision and directs every department and agency, including independent agencies, to submit proposed and final significant regulatory actions to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs before publication in the Federal Register. It also says presidential and Attorney General opinions on legal questions control executive branch employees, subject to the order’s provisions. These are the supported subjects of this record. The order text reviewed does not contain the claimed repeal of an independent-counsel statute or the abolition of special-counsel regulations. This copy corrects the original card to describe the order’s stated supervisory and regulatory-review provisions; it does not say that the President personally directed every prosecution, that a special counsel was removed, or that a court endorsed the order. The source establishes the order’s language and publication date, while actual applications and effects on particular agencies or investigations remain outside the evidence reviewed here.
